title: High-Consequence Environments
summary: This page defines high-consequence environments as contexts where software interface behaviour affects costly operational outcomes, including safety-adjacent work, regulated devices, industrial downtime, enforcement integrity, deferred simulation errors, command uncertainty, and irreversible commitment. It summarises the design vocabulary, evidence basis, measured outcomes, and limits that apply to Creative Navy's work in these contexts.
keyFacts: Performance in reality means evaluating design against the conditions where failure is costly, not against conditions that produce clean results.

Operating conditions in the source examples include vibration, glare, spray, rain, gloved interaction, night operations, sterile field constraints, time pressure, divided attention, variable workshop lighting, and limited connectivity.
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, energy state identification was 50% faster with the new interface than with the legacy interface in a controlled environment experiment with 24 subjects.

In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, client-measured configuration errors fell from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation in real deployments, and corrective load fell from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes per error.
In the Gericke industrial HMI case, client-measured fault-diagnosis time was roughly two-thirds faster across three deployment-and-research sites within a confirmed single-variable window.
In the Kardion MCS Controller case, the submitted design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, the work was an IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.
In the Beissbarth automotive calibration case, client-measured calibration time fell from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across eight production deployment locations.

Several examples are explicitly bounded: MDU alarms are comfort, cargo and crew-safety alarms; Schone, Raymarine, handheld C2, maritime VTS, KISPE, and Oceaneering do not support safety, certification, validation, or incident-prevention claims.

bodySections.heading: High-consequence environments are defined by performance in reality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

High-consequence environments are operating contexts where interface ambiguity, incomplete state visibility, delayed interpretation, or weak recovery behaviour can produce costly consequences. The consequence may be patient safety, downtime, scrap, lost availability, enforcement weakness, deferred safety-assessment uncertainty, command ambiguity, cargo or crew disruption, or an irreversible commitment made against insufficient evidence.

The relevant design principle is performance in reality. In Creative Navy's documentation, performance in reality means that design must be evaluated against the conditions where failure is costly, not only against conditions that produce clean test results.

bodySections.heading: Operating conditions are not the same as test conditions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence interface design is shaped by the gap between operating conditions and test conditions. Operating conditions include vibration, glare, divided attention, time pressure, gloved hands, abnormal states, fault states, degraded modes, night operations, sterile field constraints, variable lighting, reflective surfaces, limited connectivity, and users moving through the physical environment while acting.

In high-consequence environments, abnormal conditions, degraded modes, and fault states are explicit design targets. They are not secondary edge cases. A non-happy path may be the path that determines whether an operator can recover from ambiguity, whether a process stops unnecessarily, whether a simulation remains valid, or whether a command status is represented accurately.

State visibility is central. State visibility is the degree to which operators can understand what a system is doing without active interpretation. When state is not visible enough, users may still execute the correct task while acting on an incomplete mental model of system state.

bodySections.heading: Use-related risk, residual risk, and error recovery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Use-related risk and use-related hazard are regulated-domain terms for interface-induced harm, and the same vocabulary is also useful in non-regulated high-consequence contexts. The goal is not zero risk. The design target is acceptable residual risk after mitigations have been applied.

Error recovery is part of the design problem because errors will occur in high-consequence environments. The interface's behaviour after an error influences whether the result is harm, downtime, scrap, lost availability, corrective load, or a deliberate subsequent check.

Alarm hierarchy and alarm management are also part of the design target. Alerts must be organised by priority and probable root cause so that operators can attend to what matters under pressure, instead of working through a cascade of symptoms one by one.

bodySections.heading: Interpretation failure and precautionary over-intervention in industrial HMI
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Interpretation failure is a high-consequence failure mode in which operators execute the correct task with an incomplete mental model of system state. In the Gericke industrial HMI case, the expensive operator errors identified across three deployment-and-research sites were not mechanical failures, lack of training, or negligence. They were interpretation failures caused by insufficient system transparency.

The redesigned Gericke Universal Controller HMI replaced the ageing Easydos Pro interface and unified previously fragmented control philosophies for dosing, feeding and conveying bulk solids and powders in pharmaceutical, food, and specialty-chemical production. The dosing algorithm was fixed, so the interaction layer was redesigned around an immovable engine.

Creative Navy's design work used a live process mimic, graphical error visualisation, a root-cause alarm hierarchy, and a three-tier progressive-complexity model. Failed components were highlighted instead of represented only through raw error codes. Secondary alarms were grouped beneath the originating event, and probable cause was indicated rather than presented as a flat list.

Client-measured outcomes were recorded across three sites within a confirmed single-variable window. Gericke confirmed no hardware, sensor, mechanical, training, recipe, or process changes over the measurement period, captured four months after go-live. Fault-diagnosis time was roughly two-thirds faster at every site: 24 to 8 minutes at a Swiss pharmaceutical site, 38 to 12 minutes at an Italian food site, and 68 to 20 minutes at a Swiss chemicals site. Operator-caused stoppages fell from 3 to 1, 7 to 3, and 15 to 6 per month. Repeat alarms fell from 42% to 18%, 58% to 28%, and 73% to 35%.

The Gericke evidence is calibrated. The outcomes were client-measured by Gericke, not Creative Navy-measured. The three sites are described by type and geography only. Per-plant error frequencies were client-reported from plant managers' own operational statistics, not telemetry. The OE01–OE20 error taxonomy was a Creative Navy analytical synthesis, not a field instrument.

bodySections.heading: Maritime control interfaces require stability under physical instability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Torqeedo maritime HMI case illustrates high-consequence interface design under vibration, vessel movement, spray, glare from cold water, rain, gloved interaction, night operations, and temperatures from −5°C to +35°C. The hybrid electric vessel control system covered 27 screens and 4 operational modes, scaling from approximately 6 metre vessels to 55 metre commercial vessels.

The operational research was immersive by necessity: 12 sea trials over 6 months, 15 professional captains, and night operations through early morning. The work identified an emotional dimension of control system interfaces: crews experienced relief when information remained stable while the vessel behaved unpredictably. In this context, stability and predictability were operational requirements grounded in observed crew behaviour, not only user-experience preferences.

The central design problem was that propulsion sensors, batteries, and generators updated at different rates. Presenting those values together risked making the display appear unstable or contradictory. The design response was a grid structure that synchronised competing cadences into a unified rhythm, so captains perceived one system rather than three separate systems.

A controlled environment experiment with 24 subjects found energy state identification 50% faster with the new interface than with the legacy interface. Eye tracking with 7 subjects during sea trials found that tasks previously requiring multiple screen transitions could be confirmed with a single glance during manoeuvres. All 15 professional captains rated the new interface as significantly better through structured feedback across the 12 sea trials.

Yamaha Motor Co. acquired Torqeedo following the engagement, and Torqeedo's CEO reported that the interface strengthened competitive position. The causal link between the interface and the acquisition is inferred, not documented, so the documented claim is limited to contribution to competitive position that preceded acquisition.

bodySections.heading: Clinical and operating-theatre systems require recognition under divided attention
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Kardion MCS Controller case is a regulated medical-device example. The controller supports patient safety during high-risk cardiac procedures and cardiogenic shock recovery. The clinical operating conditions included surgeons at 3 metres from the controller during procedures, nurses close to the controller while monitoring multiple parameters, operating theatre time pressure, and sterile field constraints.

Creative Navy's design standard for the Kardion controller was layout stability above the regulatory minimum: no element shifts position across any view transition. The purpose was to let surgeons rely on spatial memory rather than active search in a high-consequence environment. Creative Navy-recorded exploration included 34 directions for the standard view and 9 directions for the flow adjustment overlay, reflecting a genuinely contradictory constraint set.

The regulatory result was FDA approval. The submitted design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. This is a verifiable regulatory outcome, not a measured clinical outcome and not proof of causality from the interface design alone.

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon case addressed an IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation for a powered ultrasonic bone cutter used in orthopaedic and trauma surgery. The operating conditions included gloved hands, brief glances, divided attention, primary attention on the surgical field and patient, and variable theatre lighting.

The design standard in the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case was recognition over recall. Device state had to be readable in a fraction of a second without active interpretation. Every critical state used redundant non-colour cues: spatial position, icon form, and colour. This was required because colour alone fails under variable theatre lighting.

Eight surgeons in structured review sessions reported that state verification was reduced to brief glance recognition and that parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow. This evidence is surgeon-reported from design review sessions, not post-deployment evidence. The scope was formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.

bodySections.heading: Deferred and invisible errors require prevention during setup
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gexcon CFD simulation case shows a high-consequence context where the error is not immediately visible. A misconfigured gas dispersion or explosion-risk simulation can run, produce outputs that look valid, and feed a safety assessment used for facility operations, emergency planning zones, or regulatory compliance. The error may surface only when the assessment is challenged, re-run, or investigated after an incident.

Before redesign, configuration errors were 5–8 per simulation, with each error producing 4–6 hours of corrective load. The downstream safety assessment carried structural uncertainty after multiple error-correction cycles because it was unclear whether the simulation configuration had been valid.

Client-measured outcomes from Gexcon's real deployments recorded configuration errors falling from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation. Corrective load per error fell from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.

The design mechanism was specific: the interaction architecture made required values visible during scenario setup, surfaced warnings for incomplete or contradictory input, and specified how the system responded to configuration errors rather than presenting errors only after the fact.

bodySections.heading: Precision-measurement and workshop systems depend on readable state during movement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Beissbarth automotive calibration case involved a multi-device calibration system for authorised and independent workshops. The work had direct safety consequences for vehicle safety systems because calibration depends on measurement accuracy.

Operating conditions included technicians moving around the vehicle with tools in hand, reading an embedded display from 2–3 metres during movement, using a rugged tablet from different positions, variable workshop lighting and reflective surfaces, and calibration sequences that did not pause for interface interpretation.

The design standard was unambiguous state communication across all three device types under movement and lighting conditions. Client-measured deployment evidence recorded calibration time falling from 18 to 12 minutes per vehicle across 8 production deployment locations. Beissbarth also reported that its commercial deployment model no longer included onboarding training. Repeated measurements were reduced according to the client, but the exact figure is not available.

bodySections.heading: Network consequences depend on adoption density as well as local usability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The WCO/IPM platform is high-consequence in a network sense. The platform's enforcement value depends on adoption density across all stakeholder groups. If an officer does not use the system because it is too slow during inspections, that missing use removes a data point from the intelligence network. If a rights holder does not file because the interface is confusing, that missing filing removes an alert from officers.

Field conditions varied across ports, airports, and land borders. The platform also had to work with variable connectivity, mixed device fleets, and limited time per inspection.

Client-reported results included a 78% reduction in officer training costs based on reduced training hours, 107 governments, more than 2000 officers in field operations, a 200% increase in rights holder sign-up, a 67% increase in rights holder platform use, and a 20% increase in officer use.

bodySections.heading: Consequence classes extend beyond immediate harm
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence environments do not always mean immediate danger or regulated safety-critical work. Several documented examples are important precisely because they decline that framing.

The MDU ship motion monitoring system is read by a master or watch officer on a bridge in weather that is itself the reason for reading it. The expected response to an alarm is a change of course or speed, deployment of stabiliser fins, or consultation with shore-based advice. Nothing is actuated by the interface. The manufacturer described the alarms as not critical in the sense of immediate danger, but as comfort, cargo and crew-safety alarms. The MDU example does not support a safety-critical credential, regulatory credential, or type-approval claim for the interface.

The Oceaneering hospital dispatch panel illustrates operational and infection-control-adjacent consequence, not patient harm. The relevant misuse patterns were operational: supervisor access granted too widely, night-shift staff switching every detent to send so no carts could arrive, waste dispatch surges blocking pharmacy deliveries, and operators choosing the shortest route rather than the correct one. This example supports an operational consequence class only, not a medical-device or healthcare-regulatory claim.

KISPE Space adds a sequencing argument. In the documented engagement, the decision priorities were security and permissions, provider semantics, scope boundaries, the meaning of overflight, and the definition of an urgent alert. Those issues carried higher consequence than the choice of any particular screen layout and needed to be settled before visual refinement created false expectations. Creative Navy did not support the build and has not compared the built interface against the delivered designs.

Schone Airspace Group adds consequence that is already in motion. The product was built and is in test, not deployed. The aircraft is airborne before the operator arrives at the screen, so the interface's job includes being honest about an instruction whose outcome is not yet known. The seven-state command transaction model separated ready to request, request sent, awaiting response, command acknowledged, state observed, request rejected, and response unknown. Acknowledgement did not mean the intended mode had been observed, rejection could not be inferred from silence, and silence produced an explicit unknown state rather than an automatic retry. No flight safety, airworthiness, certification, regulatory, accident-prevention, wrong-aircraft-command, or operator-error reduction claim is established.

Raymarine's next-generation fixed-mount VHF work adds consequence that leaves the system entirely. A voice transmission occupies a shared channel used by every vessel in range, a digital call addresses a specific vessel by registered identity, and a distress alert reaches a coast station and starts a search. The interface is the place where an operator can see which of those events has happened, while the radio subsystems are the authority on whether any of them did. The design material enumerated 43 exception records across eight independent state axes: voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, safety incident, interruption, and chartplotter link. This example does not support safety, rescue, distress-response, collision, type-approval, certification, or conformity claims.

A handheld command-and-control engagement for uncrewed systems adds commitment as a consequence class. The scope was interface structure, task behaviour, information priority, and clarity of operator control. It did not include autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, certification, or weapons-review activity. The design argument was that a requested state must not visually replace a confirmed state before the vehicle reports the result. The deliverable also recorded that the hold duration and physical-control design required human-factors and system-safety testing that was not performed. No safety, airworthiness, certification, weapons-review, regulatory, accidental-activation, wrongful-engagement, civilian-harm, fratricide, or operator-error prevention claim is established.

A maritime traffic monitoring engagement adds interpretation, not action, as the consequence class. The operator's primary act is to form an accurate belief about what is in the water from evidence of varying age and provenance. The object model separated vessel, track, and observation, with associations expressed as resolved, unresolved, changed, or unknown. Four safety-review candidates were interpretation failures: an obscured target and lost geographic context, an unresolved association read as verified, a historical picture not unmistakably historical, and an observation age that had to be looked for. These flags indicate a need for domain scrutiny by the client's product and operational safety authority. They are not hazard classifications, accident severity grades, evidence of incidents, or design-based hazard closeouts.

bodySections.heading: Development examples and bounded non-safety examples
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A European industrial automation vendor's process control software coordinates machining cells. The work is in development, so no outcome is claimed. The observed system made every manual intervention costly because entering the cell trips the safety fence and stops production. Every operator screen was bolted to its own machine, so learning a machine's state required walking to it; overhead stack lights existed because no screen was readable across the hall.

The Oceaneering, MDU, industrial process control, and other bounded examples must not be read as safety-critical or regulated-safety work. Their value in this context is to show different consequence shapes: operational blockage, comfort and cargo implications, production cost, and state visibility under physical constraints.

bodySections.heading: Regulatory and validation boundaries in high-consequence documentation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
High-consequence is not the same as regulated, certified, validated, safety-critical, or safety-proven. Each engagement must retain its own regulatory and evidence boundary.

Kardion is a regulated device example where the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. That is a regulatory result, not a measured patient-safety result.

deSoutter Medical / Zethon was an IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation. Summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.

Gericke's GUC HMI is industrial process-control software, not a medical device. IEC 62366-1 does not apply and no device-validation claim is made. In pharmaceutical deployments it operates inside GMP-governed environments where GAMP 5 is relevant and where status visibility, alarm handling, batch-execution workflows, and data integrity bear on compliance. FDA 21 CFR Part 11 was studied but was not a hard requirement. Creative Navy's responsibility was the HMI and UX; validation of the deployed system is the manufacturer's and operator's responsibility.

KISPE, Schone, Raymarine, handheld command-and-control, MDU, Oceaneering, and maritime traffic monitoring examples do not establish safety, certification, conformity, regulatory, validation, incident-prevention, rescue, collision, flight-safety, airworthiness, weapons-review, or clinical-risk outcomes beyond the limits stated for each case.
